extracted.subtask_description: A Bernays-derived rubric for crafting press releases that do not merely announce but create news — emphasizing overt acts, third‑party authority, dramatization, audience segmentation, and coordination across channels. Intended to evaluate or produce press‑release‑grade publicity that editors will pick up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overt-act test
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release report an act (an event that has actually occurred or is staged to occur) rather than an abstract claim or opinion? Per Lippmann (whom Bernays quotes), only an 'overt act' is hard enough to be reported as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concrete actions (ceremonies, awards, staged events, records) over assertions of belief or opinion. Anti-pattern: releases that consist primarily of argumentative prose or unverifiable claims. Scoring note: a named, timeable act scores high; vague intentions score low.

rubrics_metrics.name: News creation, not mere announcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Has the source manufactured a concrete, demonstrable occurrence (an award, a survey, a coalition, an institutional ceremony) that gives editors something to point to?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the release around an observable occurrence that can be independently referenced. Examples: a newly commissioned survey with headline findings, the inauguration of an advisory council, the presentation of an award. Avoid: announcements that only restate positions without a demonstrable event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release foreground respected outside figures — physicians, academics, civic leaders, opinion leaders — rather than the client's own self-praise?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite and feature external authorities as spokespeople or endorsers to lend credibility. Use quotations, signed statements, or event presence from such figures. Anti-pattern: releases dominated by the client's promotional language and self-attributed accolades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience segmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the message tailored to the psychology of distinct publics (lay readers, legislators, specialists), with separate framings/data packages for each?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare variant leadlines, fact-boxes, and supporting materials aimed at different audiences (trade press vs. general newspapers vs. policymakers). Scoring: a single release that simultaneously supplies angles for trade editors, lay readers, and policymakers scores highest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repackaging of existing material
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release take pre-existing studies, reports, or expert opinion and reformulate it so its importance is felt and appreciated, not merely available?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn dry research into a news peg — highlight a striking statistic, create a human-interest vignette, or present a novel synthesis. Avoid simply attaching reports without translating their significance into a timely, newsworthy narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatization of abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the underlying idea translated into a vivid concrete demonstration (an institution, a ceremony, a record, a 'first') rather than left as a proposition?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft visuals or staged moments that make an abstract claim tangible (e.g., a public demonstration, an exhibit, a visible record-setting). Editors favor imagery and scenes they can describe; abstract policy arguments without dramatization are less likely to be picked up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with existing public values
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release attach the client's interest to a value the public already holds, rather than asking readers to adopt a new one?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the action in terms of widely held values (health, safety, civic pride, fairness) rather than narrow commercial motives. Scoring note: framing as public benefit rather than private gain increases editorial receptivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-channel coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the printed release part of a coordinated push across the spoken, the staged, the visualized, and the mailed — i.e. is the release one prong of an integrated campaign?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the release is timed with events, speeches, visual materials, mailed materials, and other channels so that multiple touchpoints reinforce the story. Anti-pattern: sending a solo press release without supporting actions or materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visible group action / consensus signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release make a coordinated stance by many actors visible at once, so the very fact of unanimity becomes the story?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show collective endorsement (coalitions, multiple signatories, panels) to create the news angle of consensus. Presenting many actors together or simultaneous statements increases perceived importance and newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-interest framing over private gain
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release describe the action in terms of community welfare rather than commercial advantage?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize benefits to the public or specific publics; downplay overt commercial self-interest. Editors are more likely to run items that read as serving common good rather than advertising a product or service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous adaptation to opinion shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the message calibrated to the current state of public opinion (recent events, prevailing mood) rather than a stale or generic posture?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time and angle releases to prevailing news cycles and public sentiment. Update framing, examples, and spokespeople to reflect recent developments. A release that ignores the present context will feel out-of-date and score lower.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Underneath the staging, do the claims rest on verifiable fact? Bernays insists sustainable influence requires a real factual foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure claims can be corroborated with facts, data, or named sources. While events may be staged for news value, fabrications undermine long-term credibility. Scoring: releases with factual verifiability score markedly higher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grader heuristics / scoring notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristics for graders: a 'pickup-worthy' Bernaysian release names a concrete overt act, attaches it to third-party authority, and frames it as serving a public the editor's audience already cares about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these shorthand checks when evaluating: - Does it name a concrete overt act? - Does it foreground credible third-party authorities rather than client self-praise? - Does it frame the act as serving existing public values? Releases that argue without supplying an act or that lead with client self-promotion score low on overt-act and public-interest tests. Multi-public segmentation (satisfying trade editors, lay readers, and policymakers simultaneously) is a strong indicator of high pickup potential.
